notes:
Task and constraints: Return the shortest subarray whose length equals the array's degree.
Idea: Count value frequencies and remember each value's first and last positions.
Technique and why it applies: The degree is the maximum frequency. For each value with that frequency, its shortest covering span is right[value]-left[value]+1; the minimum such span is returned.
Invariant: counts holds each value's frequency, while left and right hold its earliest and latest indices.
Edge cases: The code assumes nums is nonempty because max(counts.values()) is called. Repeated values update only the right endpoint after their first occurrence.
Complexity: One pass builds the maps and a second expression scans distinct values, giving O(n) expected time and O(u) space.

Task and constraints: Merge accounts that share email addresses into one account with sorted unique emails.
Idea: Repeatedly merge accounts with the same name when their email sets overlap.
Technique and why it applies: Each account's emails are deduplicated and sorted; shared emails trigger a union of the email sets. Repeating merge until stable attempts to propagate transitive overlaps.
Invariant: ls tracks account indices already absorbed during the current merge pass, and temp holds the combined account being built.
Edge cases: The approach only compares accounts with matching names, so shared emails under different names are not merged. It can also be inefficient due to repeated full passes and set construction.
Complexity: Repeated merging can take multiple O(A²E) passes for A accounts and E emails; space is proportional to the accumulated email sets.

Task and constraints: Combine accounts that share any email, returning each merged email list sorted with its account name.
Idea: Assign an ID to each unique email and union all emails belonging to the same account.
Technique and why it applies: A shared email gets the same ID across accounts; union operations connect all emails in one account. Afterward, emails are grouped by their representative and sorted.
Invariant: UnionFind's parent array represents email connectivity, and email_to_name maps each unique email to its associated name.
Edge cases: The code assumes every account contains at least one email because it accesses account[1]. If the same email is associated with different names, the first recorded name is retained.
Complexity: With E unique emails and A account-email links, union-find work is near O(A α(E)), sorting groups adds O(E log E), and storage is O(E).

Task and constraints: Remove line and block comments from source code while preserving code that spans lines across block comments.
Idea: Scan characters while maintaining whether a block comment is open and accumulate non-comment text.
Technique and why it applies: Outside a block, /* starts a block comment and // skips the rest of the line. Inside a block, */ closes it. A line is emitted only when nonempty and not still inside a block comment.
Invariant: inComment records whether the scanner is inside a block comment, and new_str accumulates surviving characters for the current logical line.
Edge cases: A block comment may span lines, so new_str is retained while inComment remains true. Empty lines after removal are omitted.
Complexity: Each source character is scanned once, giving O(T) time and O(T) space for the accumulated output.

Task and constraints: Remove C-style line and block comments from a list of source lines.
Idea: Use a state flag for block comments and append surviving characters to a shared line buffer.
Technique and why it applies: The scanner skips /*...*/, stops at // outside a block, and preserves text before or after a block comment. The newline buffer is emitted only when a logical line is complete and nonempty.
Invariant: in_block tracks comment state, while newline stores the current logical line across physical source lines.
Edge cases: A block comment may begin or end mid-line or span lines. Empty results are not appended; the buffer resets only after a complete logical line.
Complexity: Each character is processed once, giving O(T) time and O(T) output/buffer space.

Task and constraints: Find an index where the sum of values to its left equals the sum to its right.
Idea: Track the remaining right sum and the accumulated left sum while scanning indices.
Technique and why it applies: Before checking index i, nums[i] is removed from right, leaving the sum strictly to its right; left contains values before i. Equality identifies the pivot.
Invariant: left is the sum before the current index and right is the sum after it.
Edge cases: The first valid pivot is returned. Empty input returns -1 because the loop does not run.
Complexity: The total sum and scan take O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Return the first pivot index whose left-side sum equals its right-side sum.
Idea: Compute the total once and maintain a running left sum.
Technique and why it applies: At index i, the right sum is total-left_sum-num. If it equals left_sum, i is a pivot; otherwise num is added to the left sum before advancing.
Invariant: left_sum equals the sum of all values at indices smaller than i.
Edge cases: Empty input returns -1. Negative values are handled because the equality uses arithmetic sums rather than positivity assumptions.
Complexity: One sum pass and one scan give O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Parse a chemical formula and return atom counts in sorted element-name order.
Idea: Use a stack of element-count dictionaries for parenthesized groups and parse element names, counts, and multipliers.
Technique and why it applies: Opening parentheses push a new dictionary; closing parentheses pop it and multiply its counts into the parent. Element tokens add their count to the current dictionary, and final output omits count one.
Invariant: Each stack dictionary accumulates atom counts for the current formula group.
Edge cases: The code assumes a valid formula with balanced parentheses and element symbols in standard capitalization. It relies on the element branch to add an implicit one when no numeric count follows.
Complexity: Each formula character is parsed a constant number of times, giving O(n) expected time and O(n) stack/map space.

Task and constraints: Count atoms in a valid chemical formula and serialize the counts alphabetically.
Idea: Tokenize element symbols, numbers, and parentheses with a regular expression, then combine counts using a stack of Counters.
Technique and why it applies: Elements increment the current group; opening parentheses push a fresh Counter; closing parentheses multiply the popped group by the following number and merge it into its parent.
Invariant: stk[-1] contains atom counts for the currently open group, and the outer Counter accumulates the full formula.
Edge cases: The parser assumes valid input. Multi-digit counts and nested groups are handled by the regex and multiplier conversion.
Complexity: Regex tokenization and stack merging take O(n) expected time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Return all self-dividing numbers in the inclusive range [left,right].
Idea: Convert each candidate to text, reject any containing zero, and test divisibility by every digit.
Technique and why it applies: A number is self-dividing when each of its digits divides the whole number. The zero check prevents division by zero; all remaining digit tests must succeed.
Invariant: res contains exactly the qualifying candidates encountered so far.
Edge cases: The range may include one-digit values, which pass if nonzero. The code assumes nonnegative positive candidates; zero is rejected by its digit-zero check.
Complexity: For R candidates and at most D digits each, time is O(RD) and output space is O(R).

Task and constraints: List numbers in a range that are divisible by each of their own digits.
Idea: Test every number and reject it if any digit is zero or fails to divide the number.
Technique and why it applies: any() short-circuits on the first invalid digit. A number is appended only when all digit checks pass.
Invariant: Every number returned has passed the per-digit divisibility predicate.
Edge cases: The code rejects zero-containing representations and assumes positive candidates, as required for self-dividing numbers.
Complexity: Each candidate's digits are inspected at most once, so time is O(RD) and output space is O(R).

Task and constraints: Find all self-dividing numbers between left and right.
Idea: Extract decimal digits with divmod and reject a candidate if any digit is zero or does not divide the original number.
Technique and why it applies: divmod repeatedly removes the least significant digit. Every digit must divide the original num, not the shrinking n; the helper checks this condition before continuing.
Invariant: n contains the unprocessed higher digits, while num remains the candidate being tested.
Edge cases: The code assumes left is positive; for num=0, the loop would not execute and incorrectly accept it, though typical constraints use left>=1.
Complexity: Each candidate takes O(D) time for D digits, giving O(RD) total time and O(1) auxiliary space beyond output.

Task and constraints: Count distinct nonempty palindromic subsequences of a string over the alphabet a,b,c,d, modulo 10^9+7.
Idea: Memoize interval counts and process each possible outer character using its first and last occurrence in the interval.
Technique and why it applies: For each character, the earliest and latest occurrences form a palindrome of length one or two around any palindromic subsequence inside them. This avoids counting identical subsequences created by different index choices more than once.
Invariant: memo[(start,end)] stores the number of distinct palindromic subsequences within that substring.
Edge cases: Empty intervals return zero. The loop considers only a,b,c,d, relying on the problem's restricted alphabet.
Complexity: There are O(n²) interval states, and each scans a substring for character positions, giving O(n³) time and O(n²) memo space.

Task and constraints: Recolor the connected four-directional region containing the starting pixel.
Idea: Use a queue to visit cells whose original color equals the starting cell's color, recoloring them as they are processed.
Technique and why it applies: Each matching neighbor is queued, and changing a processed cell to the new color prevents it from qualifying again when the new color differs from the target.
Invariant: The queue contains cells discovered in the target-color component, and image cells already processed hold the replacement color.
Edge cases: If color equals the starting color, the method returns immediately. deque is used but not imported in the snippet, so it requires an external definition.
Complexity: Each cell in the component is processed a bounded number of times, giving O(RC) worst-case time and O(RC) queue space.

Task and constraints: Recolor the connected region of the starting pixel with a new color.
Idea: Run recursive DFS from the start, changing matching cells and visiting their four orthogonal neighbors.
Technique and why it applies: The helper stops at boundaries or cells whose color differs from the original target. Recoloring before recursing marks the cell visited and prevents cycles.
Invariant: Every cell changed to newColor has already been visited; unmodified target-color neighbors remain candidates.
Edge cases: If the new color already matches the target, the original image is returned without traversal. The code assumes a nonempty rectangular image.
Complexity: The DFS visits each connected component cell once, giving O(RC) worst-case time and O(RC) recursion space.

Task and constraints: Simulate collisions among asteroids moving in opposite directions and return the survivors in order.
Idea: Maintain a stack and resolve collisions only when a positive asteroid is followed by a negative one.
Technique and why it applies: The smaller asteroid is popped; if the stack top is larger, it survives and destroys the incoming asteroid. Equal magnitudes destroy both. Same-direction asteroids never collide.
Invariant: stack contains the surviving asteroids from the processed prefix in their original order.
Edge cases: Zero is not expected. The while-else structure appends the incoming asteroid only if no collision branch breaks the loop.
Complexity: Each asteroid is pushed and popped at most once, giving O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Return the asteroids that survive collisions under directional and size rules.
Idea: Process asteroids from left to right using a stack of survivors.
Technique and why it applies: A collision is possible only when the stack top moves right and the new asteroid moves left. Smaller right-moving asteroids are popped until the incoming asteroid is destroyed or no collision remains.
Invariant: result is the collision-resolved sequence for the prefix processed so far.
Edge cases: Equal magnitudes remove both asteroids. The code preserves order for asteroids moving in the same direction.
Complexity: Each asteroid enters and leaves the stack at most once, so time and space are O(n).

Task and constraints: Simulate asteroid collisions and return the remaining asteroids in original order.
Idea: Append positive asteroids directly, and for each negative asteroid remove smaller positive stack tops before deciding whether it survives.
Technique and why it applies: Only a positive asteroid to the left and a negative asteroid to the right can collide. If the last positive is equal in magnitude, both disappear; if it is larger, the incoming negative is discarded.
Invariant: result stores the surviving sequence from the processed prefix.
Edge cases: A negative asteroid survives when no positive stack top remains. Equal magnitudes remove the top and do not append the incoming asteroid.
Complexity: Each asteroid is appended and removed at most once, giving O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Evaluate a Lisp-like expression containing integers, variables, add, mult, and let forms with lexical scoping.
Idea: Tokenize the expression character by character, evaluate nested parenthesized expressions, and save the variable environment when entering a nested form.
Technique and why it applies: add and mult evaluate two operands; let updates variable bindings in sequence. A stack of prior token buffers and environment copies restores the outer scope after a nested expression closes.
Invariant: lookup contains the current variable bindings, while stk stores the enclosing parser state and its environment snapshot.
Edge cases: The parser assumes syntactically valid expressions. Copying lookup on each nesting level isolates inner bindings from the surrounding scope.
Complexity: Parsing is O(n) in expression length aside from environment-copy costs; nested scope snapshots can require O(n²) total copying in deep expressions.

Task and constraints: Find the largest integer no greater than n whose decimal digits are non-decreasing.
Idea: Scan adjacent digits and, at the first descent, decrement the left digit and fill all following positions with 9s.
Technique and why it applies: Decrementing the first digit of a descending pair may create a new descent with its predecessor, so the loop backs over equal digits before decrementing. Replacing the suffix with 9s maximizes the result under the corrected prefix.
Invariant: Before the first descent, digits are non-decreasing; after repair, the prefix is reduced at the earliest safe position and the suffix is maximal.
Edge cases: If no descent exists, n is returned unchanged. The input is nonnegative and converted to a digit list.
Complexity: The scan and suffix construction are O(d) time and O(d) space for d digits.
